units.translation: ⟦1⟧ asyndetic, like ⟦2⟧ ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧⟦5⟧. All these are chosen from the noblest families; hence ⟦6⟧. Compare, moreover, how in the Frogs Aeschylus himself is escorted (1520 ff.): ⟦7⟧, ⟦8⟧. With the following verses (1028 f.) the ⟦9⟧ are addressed, and according to Robert (Hermes 38, 634 ff.) the purple garments (1028) are to be put on the Eumenides by them, which also involved a change of masks; for in their original costume and with their original face masks they could hardly enter their new abodes as deities worthy of veneration. Since the orchestra was so exceptionally full, the necessary concealment from the spectators could easily be effected. A pause, however, not filled by words, after 1031 has even less difficulty than after 234. But now the speech of Athena is commonly regarded as transmitted with a lacuna, because, so it seems, according to credible and definite testimony something formerly stood in the tragedy and now does not, which belonged at this point. See the hypothesis: (Athena) ⟦10⟧. Harpocration ⟦11⟧: ⟦12⟧, ⟦13⟧, ⟦14⟧, ⟦15⟧, ⟦16⟧. Even if one wished to derive this passage from the hypothesis instead of from the play, the first testimony would still remain, and the matter speaks for it; for that the renaming which actually did occur took place only in the title does not seem exactly credible. G. Hermann therefore placed the lacuna after 1027, also because of the asyndeton, which, however, one could easily remove (Robert): ⟦17⟧ ⟨⟦18⟧'⟩; Robert, on the other hand, after 1031, and he also gathers further material besides the change of name: thus the forgiveness for Orestes mentioned by the Eumenides (see above, Harpocration), for which, to be sure, words of Athena without an answer from those granting forgiveness would not suffice. Consider, however: if sense and construction after 1027 indicate no lacuna, then after 1031 they indicate none at all; I therefore do not venture to set the signs of one. –
show then you for this man sacred torches
and escort him with his own limbs and songs, celebrating
having appeased the Erinyes she addressed them as Eumenides
having spoken about the trial of Orestes
he says that Athena, having appeased the Erinyes
so that they were not angry with Orestes
⟦1⟧ 1028 Hermann compares with ⟦2⟧, Tro. 257 and with ⟦3⟧ ⟦4⟧.
